question.text:
Suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function such that \[ f(1,3)=4, \quad f_x(1,3)=2, \quad f_y(1,3)=1. \]

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,3),$ estimate the value of $f(1.02,3.02).$
question.explanation:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) \approx f(a,b) + \nabla f(a,b)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b \rangle. \]

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,3)$ is \begin{align} f(x,y) & \approx f(1,3) + \nabla f(1,3)\cdot \langle x-1, y-3 \rangle\\[5pt] &= f(1,3) + \langle f_x(1,3), f_y(1,3)\rangle \cdot \langle x- 1, y-3 \rangle \\[5pt] & = 4 + \langle 2, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle x-1, y-3 \rangle . \end{align}

We can approximate $f(1.02,3.02)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x= 1.02$ and $y=3.02,$ as follows: \begin{align} f(1.02,3.02) &\approx 4 + \langle 2, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle 1.02-1, 3.02-3 \rangle\\[3pt] &= 4 + \langle 2, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle 0.02, 0.02 \rangle\\[3pt] & = 4 + 0.04 + 0.02 \\[3pt] & = 4.06 \end{align}

question.text:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that \[ f(-1,1) = 3, \quad f_x(x,y)= 4x, \quad f_y(x,y) = 2y. \]

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,1),$ estimate the value of $f(-0.95, 0.95).$
question.explanation:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) \approx f(a,b) + \nabla f(a,b)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b \rangle. \]

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,1)$ is \begin{align} f(x,y) & \approx f(-1,1) + \nabla f(-1,1) \cdot \langle x + 1, y - 1\rangle\\[5pt] & = f(-1,1) + \langle f_x(-1,1) , f_y(-1,1)\rangle \cdot \langle x + 1, y - 1 \rangle\\[5pt] & = 3 + \langle f_x(-1,1), f_y(-1,1) \rangle \cdot \langle x + 1, y - 1 \rangle . \end{align}

Now, we find $f_x(-1,1)$ and $f_y(-1,1)$ using the given partial derivatives: \begin{align} f_x(-1,1) & = 4(-1) = -4 \\[5pt] f_y(-1,1) & = 2(1) = 2 \end{align}

Therefore, we have \[ f(x,y) \approx 3 + \langle -4, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle x + 1, y - 1\rangle. \]

Finally, we can estimate $f(-0.95, 0.95)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x = -0.95$ and $y = 0.95,$ as follows: \begin{align} f(-0.95, 0.95) & \approx 3 + \langle -4, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle -0.95 + 1, 0.95 - 1\rangle\\[5pt] & = 3 + \langle -4, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle 0.05, -0.05 \rangle \\[5pt] & = 3 - 0.2 - 0.1 \\[5pt] & = 2.7 \end{align}

question.text: Suppose that $f(x,y, z)$ is a differentiable function such that \[ f(1,-1,2)=6, \quad f_x(1,-1,2)=-4, \quad f_y(1,-1,2)=-1, \quad f_z(1,-1,2)=3. \] Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,2)$ estimate the value of $f(1.04,-0.99,2.02).$
question.explanation:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b, c)$ is given by \[ f(x,y,z) \approx f(a,b,c) + \nabla f(a,b,c)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b,z-c \rangle. \]

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1,2)$ is \[ \begin{align} f(x,y,z) & \approx f(1,-1,2) + \nabla f(1,-1,2)\cdot \langle x-1, y+1,z-2 \rangle\\[5pt] &= f(1,-1,2) + \langle f_x(1,-1,2), f_y(1,-1,2), f_z(1,-1,2)\rangle \cdot \langle x-1, y+1,z-2 \rangle \\[5pt] & = 6 + \langle -4,-1,3 \rangle \cdot \langle x-1, y+1,z-2 \rangle. \end{align} \]

We can approximate $f(1.04,-0.99,2.02)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x= 1.04,$ $y=-0.99,$ and $z=2.02$ as follows:

\[ \begin{align} f(1.04,-0.99,2.02) &\approx 6 +\langle -4, -1,3 \rangle \cdot \langle 1.04 - 1, -0.99+1,2.02-2 \rangle \\[5pt] & = 6+ \langle -4,-1,3 \rangle \cdot \langle 0.04, 0.01,0.02 \rangle \\[5pt] & = 6 - 0.16 -0.01 + 0.06 \\[5pt] & = 5.89 \end{align} \]

example.title: Estimating the Value of a Three-Variable Function

question.text:
Suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function such that \[ f(2,0) = 0, \quad f_x(2,0) = 0, \quad f_y(2,0) = 2. \]

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,0),$ estimate the value of $f(2.01,0.02).$
question.explanation:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) \approx f(a,b) + \nabla f(a,b)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b \rangle. \]

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,0)$ is \begin{align} f(x,y) & \approx f(2,0) + \nabla f(2,0) \cdot \langle x - 2, y - 0 \rangle\\[5pt] & = f(2,0) + \langle f_x(2,0), f_y(2,0)\rangle \cdot \langle x - 2, y \rangle \\[5pt] & = 0 + \langle 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle x - 2, y \rangle\\[5pt] & = \langle 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle x - 2, y \rangle. \end{align}

We can approximate $f(2.01 , 0.02)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x = 2.01$ and $y = 0.02,$ as follows: \begin{align} f(2.01 , 0.02) & \approx \langle 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle 2.01 - 2, 0.02 \rangle\\[5pt] &= \langle 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle 0.01, 0.02 \rangle\\[5pt] & = 0(0.01) + 2(0.02) \\[5pt] & = 0 + 0.04\\[5pt] & = 0.04 \end{align}

question.text: Suppose that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function such that \[ f(1,-1) = -2, \quad f_x(1,-1) = 1, \quad f_y(1,-1) = 6. \] Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1),$ estimate the value of $f(0.96,-0.95).$
question.explanation:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by \[ f(x,y) \approx f(a,b) + \nabla f(a,b)\cdot \langle x-a, y-b \rangle. \]

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-1)$ is \begin{align} f(x,y) & \approx f(1,-1) + \nabla f(1,-1) \cdot \langle x - 1, y - (-1) \rangle\\[5pt] & = f(1,-1) + \langle f_x(1,-1), f_y(1,-1)\rangle \cdot \langle x - 1, y + 1 \rangle \\[5pt] & = -2 + \langle 1, 6 \rangle \cdot \langle x - 1, y + 1\rangle \end{align}

We can approximate $f(0.96,-0.95)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x = 0.96$ and $y = -0.95,$ as follows: \begin{align} f(0.96 , -0.95) & \approx -2 + \langle 1, 6 \rangle \cdot \langle 0.96 - 1, -0.95 + 1 \rangle\\[5pt] & = -2 + \langle 1, 6 \rangle \cdot \langle -0.04, 0.05 \rangle\\[5pt] & = -2 + 1(-0.04) + 6(0.05) \\[5pt] & = -2 - 0.04 + 0.3\\[5pt] & = -1.74 \end{align}
